description_full: BorgWarner Inc., together with its subsidiaries, provides technology solutions for combustion, hybrid, and electric vehicles worldwide. The company operates through the Turbos & Thermal Technologies; Drivetrain & Morse Systems; PowerDrive Systems; and Battery & Charging Systems segments. It offers turbochargers, eBoosters, eTurbos, emissions systems, thermal systems, gasoline ignition technology, smart remote actuators, powertrain sensors, cabin heaters, battery heaters, and battery cooling systems. The company also provides chain systems and variable camshaft phasing products; friction and mechanical products for automatic transmissions, including dual clutch modules, friction clutch modules, electromagnetic clutches, friction and separator plates, transmission bands, torque converter clutches, one-way clutches, and torsional vibration dampers; hydraulic controls products for automatic transmissions, such as electro-hydraulic solenoids for standard and hydraulic systems, transmission solenoid modules and dual clutch hydraulic control modules; and torque management products comprising transfer cases and couplings; electronic limited slip differentials, electric torque vectoring products, and axle disconnect systems. In addition, it offers power electronics, including inverters, onboard chargers, DC/DC converters, and combination boxes; rotating electric machines comprising eMotors and generators; fully integrated drive modules consisting of inverters and gear reducers; and electronic controls, such as engine control units, transmission control units, battery management systems, propulsion controllers, and domain controllers. Further, the company provides battery and charging systems, including nickel manganese cobalt battery packs and lithium iron phosphate battery packs. BorgWarner Inc. was formerly known as Borg-Warner Automotive, Inc. The company was founded in 1928 and is headquartered in Auburn Hills, Michigan.

financial_summary: BorgWarner Inc. is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $10.2B market cap on $14.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -3% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.

Returns on capital run at 8% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, and 20% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $1.2B in free cash flow — roughly 8 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 5.95× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.1× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 5.4×.

Management returns a meaningful 6.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.5× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sector_headwinds.text: Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Altman Z in the grey zone — financial health warrants monitoring
Insiders are net sellers (93% sell ratio, net $8.8M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Revenue growth lags most Consumer Cyclical peers — losing share inside the profit pool
Consumer demand is fundamentally cyclical — a recession compresses both unit volume and pricing power, and operating leverage cuts both ways.
E-commerce margin compression and tariff exposure — digital competition erodes pricing power while trade policy reshuffles supply-chain cost structures overnight.
Brand relevance decay — shifting consumer preferences and social-media-driven trends can strand inventory and invalidate positioning faster than product cycles can adapt.

Valued at a 44% discount to sector median EV/EBITDA
Piotroski score 7/9 — financials improving across profitability, leverage and efficiency
13 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
Consumer Cyclical sector outperforming the broader market over the past quarter

sect: Its 4% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Cyclical median (7%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.47x its revenue share).
It accounts for 0.3% of sector revenue and 0.1% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-16.2% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 35% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 25% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 35% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 43% and a beta of 0.93, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $135.0M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 55% in the 2020 crash, 36% in the 2022 bear market and 72% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 61% below its DCF fair value of $129, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 46%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $91.07 to $185 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Cyclical peers: EV/EBITDA 5.9 vs 10.7 and P/FCF 8.7 vs 16.7 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 174% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 11.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The 15 covering analysts target $77.93 on average, 53% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 8% earns above the cost of capital of 7.8%, but the 0pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.53).
It runs a 20% gross margin and converts 8% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9.
ROE of 5% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 5.0% of revenue on R&D and 0.5% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.1x net debt to EBITDA ($1.6B of cash against $3.9B of debt), with interest covered 5.4x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -3.2% over 3 years, 7.1% over 5 years and 6.0% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 15%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 7.9% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 9.7% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (3.3% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 15, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.6%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 14 sales over the past year, net $8.8M sold.
It returns 6.1% a year to shareholders (5.0% in buybacks and 1.3% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.8% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 13 consecutive years, though it has been cut 4.0% a year over the last five.
people: With about 37,500 employees, each generates about $382K of revenue, in line with the Consumer Cyclical median, and revenue has grown 8.4% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $31K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.9M (13x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
